exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with night‑time tingling in the little finger that improves when he straightens his elbow – what bedside test confirms the diagnosis? — Perform Tinel’s sign over the cubital tunnel and the elbow flexion test; a positive result supports CuTS.

During a ward round you note wasting of the first dorsal interosseous muscle – which nerve is involved and what does this indicate about severity? — The ulnar nerve; muscle wasting signifies moderate to severe disease requiring early surgical referral.

A patient with HIV on antiretroviral therapy develops ulnar neuropathy – how does this affect your differential? — Consider HIV‑related neuropathy as a contributing factor; still assess for mechanical compression and treat both causes.

You have no access to nerve conduction studies; how do you decide whether to operate? — Rely on clinical severity (persistent weakness, muscle wasting) and failure of 3‑6 months of conservative therapy.
What complication should you monitor for after ulnar nerve transposition surgery? — Post‑operative scar formation causing recurrent compression; monitor for return of symptoms.

A patient with rheumatoid arthritis presents with elbow swelling and ulnar symptoms – what additional investigation is essential? — Plain elbow X‑ray to look for joint erosions or osteophytes that may exacerbate compression.

Why are NSAIDs preferred over steroids for initial management in low‑resource settings? — NSAIDs reduce inflammation without the immunosuppression risk of steroids, which can worsen infections common in these settings.

A trainee suggests prescribing a high‑dose vitamin B12 for this neuropathy – how do you respond? — Vitamin B12 is not indicated for mechanical compression; focus on decompression and anti‑inflammatory measures.
ai.title: Cubital Tunnel Syndrome
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Cubital tunnel syndrome is ulnar nerve compression at the elbow causing sensory loss and motor weakness in the hand. Diagnosis relies on history, exam and simple bedside tests, with imaging reserved for atypical cases.

b: Diagnosis requires compatible symptoms, objective weakness or sensory loss, and a positive provocative test.
Exclude cervical radiculopathy and other peripheral neuropathies.
sections.p: Cubital tunnel syndrome (CuTS) is compression of the ulnar nerve within the cubital tunnel at the medial elbow, leading to sensory and motor deficits in its distribution.

t.b: What symptoms are present and what activities worsen them? – Identifies typical paresthesia in the ring and little fingers and aggravating elbow flexion.

t.a: Tinel’s sign over the cubital tunnel
t.b: Does tapping elicit tingling? – Positive sign supports ulnar nerve irritation.
Does prolonged flexion reproduce symptoms? – Positive test indicates dynamic compression.
Is there weakness of finger abduction/adduction or decreased sensation? – Confirms motor and sensory involvement.
What is the nerve conduction velocity across the elbow? – Slowed velocity confirms CuTS; if unavailable, rely on clinical findings.

b: Mild: intermittent paresthesia, no measurable weakness.
Moderate: persistent symptoms, mild weakness, grip strength ↓10‑20%.
Severe: marked weakness, muscle wasting of the first dorsal interosseous, functional loss.
sections.p: Severity is graded by symptom duration, degree of motor loss and functional impact.

b: Prolonged elbow flexion (sleeping with elbow bent, manual labor).
External pressure (leaning on elbows, tight casts).
Anatomical variants (prominent medial epicondyle, Osborne ligament thickening).
Trauma or fracture around the elbow.
Systemic conditions common in low‑resource settings: rheumatoid arthritis, leprosy neuropathy, HIV‑related neuropathy, sickle‑cell vaso‑occlusive crises causing edema.
sections.p: Compression can be static (anatomical narrowing) or dynamic (repetitive flexion).

b: Nighttime symptoms that improve on arm extension.
Clawing of the fourth and fifth fingers in advanced disease.
Visible wasting of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
sections.p: Patients report tingling, numbness or burning in the ulnar side of the hand, worsened by elbow flexion. Weakness of grip and finger abduction appears later.
Investigations aim to confirm nerve compression and rule out mimics.

t.b: Is there bony abnormality or joint deformity? – Detects fractures, osteophytes that may compress the nerve.
Is the ulnar nerve enlarged or displaced? – Shows dynamic compression; if unavailable, rely on clinical tests.
What is the latency across the elbow? – Prolonged latency confirms CuTS; not essential if classic presentation.

b: Rapidly progressive weakness suggesting acute trauma.
Severe muscle wasting leading to permanent loss of hand function.
Concurrent infection (e.g., septic arthritis) causing worsening compression.
Activity modification – avoid prolonged elbow flexion, use elbow pads.
Night splinting in extension – reduces dynamic compression.
NSAIDs for pain and inflammation when not contraindicated.
Physiotherapy: nerve gliding exercises, gentle stretching of the triceps.
If conservative measures fail after 3‑6 months or severe weakness present, refer for surgical decompression (simple decompression or anterior transposition).
sections.p: Initial treatment focuses on relieving pressure and addressing reversible causes; surgery is reserved for persistent or severe cases.

b: Re‑assess grip strength and sensory map every 4‑6 weeks.
Educate on ergonomic work practices and proper elbow positioning.
Monitor for recurrence after surgery; early physiotherapy reduces scar formation.
sections.p: Regular review ensures symptom resolution and prevents recurrence.

b: Cervical radiculopathy (C8‑T1) – often has neck pain and dermatomal pattern.
Guyon canal syndrome – compression at the wrist, sparing the elbow.
Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes or HIV – usually bilateral and distal.
sections.p: Conditions that mimic CuTS share ulnar distribution symptoms.

b: Normal nerve conduction study early in disease – clinical exam remains paramount.
Mild radiographic changes that do not explain symptoms – do not dismiss clinical signs.
sections.p: Certain findings may be falsely reassuring.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe pain with swelling suggesting infection
Progressive muscle wasting despite conservative care
